report:
## Conclusion

Your understanding is correct: the best available evidence indicates saw palmetto does **not** meaningfully improve BPH symptoms over placebo in the longer term.

**Key evidence:**

1. **Cochrane systematic review (Franco et al., 2023)** — the highest-quality evidence source, pooling 27 randomized trials with 4,656 men, most using validated urinary symptom scores and quality-of-life measures over months. It found that Serenoa repens (saw palmetto) alone provided "little to no benefit" compared with placebo for lower urinary tract symptoms due to benign prostatic enlargement, with more uncertainty (but no clear benefit) when combined with other herbal agents (https://www.cochrane.org/zh-hans/evidence/CD001423_serenoa-repens-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia; summarized also at https://www.urotoday.com/recent-abstracts/men-s-health/bph-benign-prostatic-enlargement/148951-serenoa-repens-for-the-treatment-of-lower-urinary-tract-symptoms-due-to-benign-prostatic-enlargement-an-updated-cochrane-review.html).

2. **CAMUS trial (NIH-funded, JAMA 2011, with follow-up dose-escalation analysis)** — a rigorous, large, multi-year, placebo-controlled trial that tested saw palmetto at standard dose and up to three times the standard dose (320–960 mg/day) for 72 weeks. Even at triple dose, it found no improvement in urinary symptoms or flow rates versus placebo, though it confirmed the extract was safe and non-toxic (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3979451/).

3. Commentary reviewing this evidence base (e.g., a men's health/urology summary) reinforces that despite decades of use and earlier, smaller, often lower-quality or industry-linked trials suggesting benefit, the largest, best-designed, longer-duration trials consistently show no meaningful difference from placebo (https://drstanfield.com/en-eu/blogs/articles/saw-palmetto-and-prostate-supplements-benefits-forms-dosing-and-side-effects).

**Bottom line:** Earlier positive results likely reflected smaller sample sizes, shorter duration, publication bias, and heterogeneous/inconsistent extracts. Rigorous, adequately powered, long-term placebo-controlled research (Cochrane review and CAMUS) shows saw palmetto is not more effective than placebo for BPH symptoms.
